messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark has come to understand his life in two distinct parts: before the festival, and after. Before, he was a 36-year-old man who worked in the receiving department of a big-box store, a job he found satisfyingly straightforward. He loved his wife, Sarah, and looked forward to the annual music festival they attended every summer. The ‘after’ began nine months ago, on a muddy field under a sky that had turned a bruised purple. When the storm hit with unexpected violence, a lighting rig collapsed into the panicked crowd. Mark was knocked from his feet, and in an instant, the world became a chaotic press of limbs and suffocating weight.

His memory of the event is not a continuous story. Instead, it exists in his mind as a series of distinct, terrible photographs. There is the image of a man’s boot, inches from his face. There is the image of the wide, terrified eyes of a young woman beside him. And there is the most persistent image: the crinkled, cheap green plastic of a poncho, pressed so hard against his cheek that he could feel the texture of it, smell its synthetic odor, and hear its rustling over his own ragged breaths. These moments feel more real to him than his memory of what he ate for breakfast this morning. When they flash into his mind, unbidden, they bring with them a hot, suffocating wave of shame. He remembers the pure, animal terror he felt, the way he just curled up and waited, doing nothing to help himself or anyone else. He was certain in those moments that he was a coward, and that shame clings to every recollection.

In the months that followed, Mark developed a series of silent rules to manage his days. He began telling himself a different story about what happened, a watered-down version where it was just a chaotic fall, not that bad, nothing to be so upset about. He would repeat this to himself when the images started to creep in at the edges of his vision. When that failed, he would try to force the thoughts out, a brute-force effort of will, clenching his fists and chanting "stop" under his breath. But the triggers were everywhere. At his job, the shrink-wrap used to secure pallets of merchandise has the same slick, crinkly texture as the poncho. Unwrapping a shipment one afternoon, the feel of the plastic under his fingers sent him stumbling back, gasping for air, the memory-photograph of the green poncho filling his entire vision.

The world now feels full of potential threats. Standing in a queue at the grocery store, the feeling of someone brushing past him from behind can trigger a jolt of panic that makes his heart hammer against his ribs. He has come to believe that people are fundamentally selfish and dangerous when pushed. This conviction makes his retail job a minefield. When he sees customers pushing impatiently past one another on a busy Saturday, or arguing with a cashier, he doesn't just see rudeness; he sees the same dark impulse that made people trample others to save themselves. The anger that rises in him is so intense he has to retreat to the stockroom, his hands shaking. It was in the stockroom, after one such incident, that he discovered a new, more effective way to stop the intrusive images. Overwhelmed by the memory and the rage, he dug his fingernails hard into his palm until the sharp, grounding pain sliced through the mental chaos. The relief was immediate and absolute. Since then, it has become his last resort, a secret he keeps hidden under long sleeves.

The strategies have taken their toll. The constant effort of suppression and avoidance has left him exhausted and irritable. The distance between him and Sarah has grown into a chasm he no longer knows how to cross. She sees his flinching, his anger, his withdrawal, but he cannot bring himself to explain it, silenced by the shame of his perceived cowardice. He finally sought help last week, after Sarah found him in the bathroom, staring at four deep, red crescent moons he had gouged into his forearm. The look of fear and confusion in her eyes was more painful than the injury itself. He is here now because he is terrified of losing her, and he is desperate for the terrible, vivid photographs in his head to finally fade, to become just memories of something that happened long ago, rather than something that is happening to him, again and again, every single day.
